chapter_theme: Manimekalai wakes alone on the island of Manipallavam, knowing neither the place nor whether she dreams, calls for Sudhamathi and suspects the goddess who brought her of deceit, then, wandering the shore, laments her father, whose death by the sword in a foreign land she lays to a cruel deed come to ripeness. Before her appears the Dharma seat placed by the king of the gods, over which two Naga kings once warred, each calling it 'ours', until the great sage stopped the war by calling it 'ours' and preached dharma from it.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, left alone on Manipallavam by the goddess Manimekala
Manimekalai's companion, left behind in Puhar's grove
the sea goddess who carried Manimekalai to the island, suspected here as the woman who appeared by sorcery
Manimekalai's father, killed by the sword in Madurai, addressed here only as ஐயா
Kovalan's wife, named here only as the woman of the round bangles
Indra, king of the gods, who set the jewelled seat on the island
two kings of one line who rule the Naga land below and fought over the seat
the Buddha, called here the virtuous one (அறவோன்) and the great sage of tapas

manimekalai:8:1-18.reading: While Manimekalai is thus carried off, on Manipallavam, an island girdled by the sea where conches plough the shore, pearls grow in the fields with red coral and pools of lily and kuvalai lie under shading punnai and screw-pine, the girl wakes on a bed of flowers in the moon-white sand and, like a life born in another place, sees neither her kin nor her town but only things she never saw, the long blue sea and the morning sun spreading its rays.
manimekalai:8:1-18.nuance: The simile at line 14, வேறு இடத்துப் பிறந்த உயிரே போன்று, compares her waking to a rebirth in a strange place, before the next kaathai makes her recover her real former birth on this very island; the waking is already shaped as a birth that has forgotten what came before. The island is drawn as a lush shore (neythal things: conch, pearl, coral, punnai, screw-pine), so her fear is not of a wasteland but of an unknown beauty.
manimekalai:8:1-18.event: Manimekalai wakes on the sands of Manipallavam at sunrise and finds neither her companions nor her town.
manimekalai:8:1-18.unit_note: The end of the printed unit 1-19 moved back one line to 18: line 18 closes the description of what she sees at sunrise, and her cry opens at line 19, so the speech is kept whole in the next unit.

manimekalai:8:19-35.reading: Manimekalai cries out asking whether this is some spot beside the Uvavanam grove, reproaches Sudhamathi for hiding and causing her pain, says she cannot tell waking from dream and begs for an answer, calls on her friend to come since the night is over and Madhavi will be distraught, wonders whether the shining woman who appeared by sorcery has tricked her, and says she fears being all alone; then she wanders everywhere over the shore and dunes, where flocks of many-coloured birds with the swan as their king gather facing one another like kings in a war camp, and finds none of her companions.
manimekalai:8:19-35.nuance: She suspects the goddess who saved her, விஞ்சையின் தோன்றிய விளங்கு இழை மடவாள் (25), of வஞ்சம்: the rescue that the story treats as providence feels to the rescued girl like a betrayal. The bird simile at 30 to 33 (a swan king, flocks massed like kings' encampments, பாசறை மன்னர் பாடி) prepares, in miniature and harmlessly, the war of the two Naga kings over the seat told at the end of the kaathai.
manimekalai:8:19-35.event: Manimekalai calls for Sudhamathi, asks whether she is dreaming, suspects the goddess of a trick, and searches the shore for her companions in vain.
manimekalai:8:19-35.unit_note: Both boundaries moved: the unit now starts at line 19, where her quoted cry begins, and ends at line 35, where காணாள் completes the sentence of her fruitless search begun at line 28 (the printed unit ended at 34 in mid-sentence, break score 1).

manimekalai:8:36-43.reading: Her hair coming loose and falling behind, she wails, calls aloud and weeps, and in her deep grief thinks of her father: the cruel deed that casts us into this misery ripened, so that he went to a foreign land with the woman of the round bangles and his jewelled chest suffered the sharp sword, and she cries 'O father!'
manimekalai:8:36-43.nuance: Her lament names no king, no goldsmith and no guard: the sword stroke is set down wholly to the ripening of a cruel deed (வெவ் வினை உருப்ப, 40), where the Silappathikaram gives both the bent sceptre and the former deed as causes. And the deed is one that afflicts 'us' (எம், 40): she counts her own abandonment on the island and her father's death as one ripening, though the text does not say whose deed it was. Kannaki is not named and not called mother, only the woman of the round bangles (கோல் தொடி மாதர், 41), though in kaathai 2 Madhavi calls Manimekalai the great pathini's daughter.
manimekalai:8:36-43.event: Wandering the shore, Manimekalai weeps and laments her father Kovalan, killed by the sword in a foreign land.

claims.claim: a cruel deed, come to ripeness, brought the father to a violent death abroad and the daughter to her present misery

manimekalai:8:36-43.unit_note: New unit cut from the printed units 35-49 and 50-63: it begins at line 36, after காணாள் ends the search, and ends at line 43, where her lament closes with ஐயாவோ என்று; line 43's அழுவோள் முன்னர் leads into the apparition of the seat that fills lines 44 to 63.

manimekalai:8:44-63.reading: Before her as she weeps there appears the Dharma seat: a jewelled seat spreading bright rays, three cubits high and nine cubits across on every side, its circle laid out by rule and topped with a lotus square, called the seat made for the virtuous one, on which trees let fall only fragrant flowers and near which birds do not beat their wings, set there by the king of the gods, a seat of dharma on which births shine clear; over it two kings of one line who rule the Naga land below, each saying 'this is ours', could neither lift it nor let go of their great attachment and with red eyes and smoking hearts made fierce war with their armies, until the great sage of tapas, saying 'cease this great war, this is ours', sat on it and preached dharma, and the noble praise it.
manimekalai:8:44-63.nuance: The kings' claim and the sage's are the same words, எமது ஈது (56, 60): the war is ended not by the sage's refusing to own but by a counter-claim made for dharma by one without attachment, which the kings' own attachment (பெரும் பற்று, 57) could not answer. The seat's peace (no fruit falls on it, no wings beat near it) is set against their red eyes and smoking hearts. பிறப்பு விளங்கு (53) is read here as 'on which births shine clear', which the next kaathai bears out when Manimekalai, worshipping at it, knows her former birth; it could also be read as praise of the seat's own origin.
manimekalai:8:44-63.event: The Dharma seat set by Indra appears before the weeping Manimekalai; the narrator tells how two Naga kings warred over it until the great sage stopped the war and preached dharma from it.

claims.claim: great attachment to possession, which cannot let go, drives kin to war
the Dharma seat on which the sage preached makes former births shine clear

manimekalai:8:44-63.unit_note: The start of the printed unit 50-63 moved back to line 44: lines 44 to 63 are one sentence describing the seat, whose finite verb is தோன்றியது at line 63, so the seat's description is kept whole.

links.note: In the next kaathai Manimekalai, remembering her former birth as Ilakkumi, recalls the sage's word that on a day of grave sorrow the goddess Manimekala would come, lift her up in the dark night and set her on an island in the south.
links.teaches: The waking that she meets as abandonment and a strange rebirth is the foretold step of a prophecy she has not yet remembered, so the epic makes her terror on the shore the unknowing half of a plan the reader learns only afterwards.

links.note: The sage's prophecy, recalled in kaathai 9, bids her go to the radiant seat where the healer of the disease of birth sits and preaches, where the Naga kings cleared anger and the stain of mind, and worship it, and that very day know her birth.
links.teaches: The seat that the narrator first presents as the prize of a war over 'ours' is named in the prophecy by what it did to the warring kings, purging their anger and opening their ears to dharma, so the place that cured possession becomes the place where a grieving girl recovers her past.

links.note: Silappathikaram 16 tells how a drunken guard's sword cut Kovalan down as the king's sceptre bent and his former deed came in wrath; his daughter's lament on the island recalls the sword on his chest and the cruel deed ripening.
links.teaches: The earlier epic gives two causes for Kovalan's death, the bent sceptre and the ripened deed, but his daughter's memory keeps only the deed and stretches it over her own plight, so the sequel's first word on the killing drops the king's guilt and makes karma something a family suffers together.

links.note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Manimekalai says the cruel deed ripened so that her father went to a foreign land and died by the sword, and that it casts 'us' into misery.
links.teaches: The quatrain's deed that hunts down its own doer explains how karma found Kovalan far from home, yet the daughter's 'us' lets the same ripening fall on her too, which the one-doer rule does not allow, so the pair opens the question whether a deed's fruit can be shared by kin.

gains.a: a stated rule that the deed seeks out its own doer, against which her claim to share her father's ripening becomes visible as a widening
gains.b: a case in which the deed finds its doer in a strange land, and a survivor who counts herself in its fruit, a limit the calf image leaves untested

links.note: Kural 350 bids one cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging in order to let clinging go; the two Naga kings, unable to let go of their great attachment to the seat each calls 'ours', stop their war when the great sage calls it 'ours' and preaches from it.
links.teaches: The couplet's paradox, giving up attachment by attaching to the unattached one, is staged as a scene: the sage does not tell the kings to own nothing but sets his own claim, 'this is ours', in place of theirs, and their war ends because a claim of the one without clinging displaces a claim of clinging.

gains.a: a doctrinal key to why the sage answers the kings with the very words of possession they used, instead of a call to give the seat up
gains.b: a concrete case of the clinging the couplet means (kin kings at war over an object neither can lift) and of the moment the substituted clinging takes hold

source_issues: The printed unit 20-34 breaks in mid-sentence (break score 1): line 19 opens Manimekalai's speech that runs to line 27, and the sentence of her search runs from 28 to காணாள் at 35; the units were re-cut at 18, 35 and 43.
Line 63 ends தோன்றியது ஆங்கு என்: the closing என் is the kaathai-ending particle, not part of the sentence.
